newsitem.title: USA: Names surface for U.S. Transportation, FAA posts.
newsitem.headline: Names surface for U.S. Transportation, FAA posts.

text.p: Names are surfacing for the positions of Transportation Secretary and head of the Federal Aviation Administration in President Clinton's second term, industry sources said this week.
Current Transportation Secretary Federico Pena has announced his intention to leave and FAA administrator David Hinson has already left.
Historically, a secretary is named first and then the administrator of the FAA, to insure the two can work together easily. The FAA is part of the Transportation Department.
The White House has said it is concentrating for now on filling vacant national security posts but among the names being mentioned for Transportation Secretary are:

- Rodney Slater, a Clinton friend from Arkansas and administrator of the Federal Highway Administration, also an arm of the Transportation Department. The naming of Slater, an African-American, would give the Cabinet the diversity Clinton says he wants.
- William Daley, brother of Chicago Mayor Richard Daley. Was passed over for Transportation Secretary in 1993 in favor of the hispanic Pena.
- Retired U.S. Rep. Norman Mineta of California, who had been headed the House Public Works and Transportation Committee, now the Transportation and Infrastructure panel.
- Former Virginia Governor Gerald Baliles, chairman of the special commission Clinton created in 1993 to try find ways to revitatize the then ailing U.S. aviation industry.
To head the FAA, political background is not needed, but aviation expertise is, both hands on and technical. Said to be in the running are:
- John Fearnsides, senior vice president and general manager of the Mitre Corp's Center for Advanced Aviation Systems Development in Washington;
- Carl Vogt, former head of the National Transportation Safty Board and former AMTRAK board member.
- Robert Baker, executive vice president for operations at American Airlines -- the carrier's number three official.
